body_markdown:
As we reported[on October 16,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/under-the-hood-of-dodgesrumored-return-to-nascar-cup/) Dodge confirmed on Monday that after 15 years away from the top stock car series, the brand will return to NASCAR Cup racing with at least a two-car team for 2027, beginning with the season-opening 2027 Daytona 500 in February.


So says Tim Kuniskis, who[returned](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/tim-kuniskis-un-retires-to-lead-ram-once-again/) after a brief retirement to re-energize the brands after the top management at parent company Stellantis[insisted that American consumers wanted electric cars and not V-8 engines](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/cnbc-stellantis-ceo-carlos-tavares-didnt-get-u-s-market-hemi-was-victim/) , which sent the company even deeper into the doldrums. Kuniskis brought back the Hemi V-8, and followed that with a 2026 return to NASCAR, but in the Craftsman Truck series, not the top-tier Cup series.


Stellantis / Kaulig Racing


The company tagged Kaulig Racing with the responsibility of launching a Ram truck program over the winter, putting five Ram NASCAR trucks on the track at this year’s Daytona kickoff. It wasn’t easy, but the situation could have been worse; all the competitive trucks in the series use a spec V-8 produced by the[Roger Penske](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/at-85-roger-penske-just-cant-stop/) –backed Ilmor Engineering. With the spec engine, transmission, and basic chassis used in the truck series, starting up a team from scratch was far easier for Kaulig than it would have been for Ram to develop all those elements independently.


Even so, this has been a character-building year for the racing Rams. In a 24-race season that ends with race 25 on Friday, the five Ram race trucks have competed in a total of 141 individual races this year, and Ram has scored just one top-five finish, from former Cup driver Justin Haley. The highest-placed Ram driver in the points is Brendan “Butterbean” Queen, who is 14th.


Allmendinger’s #16 Grizzly Nicotine Pouches/Turtlebox Chevrolet


David Jensen/Getty Images


It has also been a long season for Kaulig’s two-car Chevrolet Cup team, with driver A.J. Allmendinger 25th in points, and teammate Ty Dillon in 34th. Dillon has no top-10 finishes, while Allmendinger has four.


Next weekend, at NASCAR’s season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, Kaulig and Ram will announce who will drive the Dodge Cup cars, and possibly how many cars Kaulig hopes to field. The team owns two charters, which means that no matter how slow a car may be, two charters mean that two of a team’s cars are guaranteed a starting spot in all 36 races, a big deal when you are courting sponsors.


If Kaulig and Dodge plan to field more than two cars, they will have to enter those extras as “open” cars, meaning they will have to qualify against other non-chartered open cars for the five available starting positions, unless Dodge and Kaulig want to buy an existing charter from another team, or possibly even buy a chartered Chevrolet, Toyota, or Ford team or two and flip them to Dodge. Non-chartered teams compete for less prize money than chartered teams do.


As far as drivers go, Kaulig could retain Allmendinger and/or Dillon, or move up one or more drivers from the Ram truck program. And the rumor persists that Brad Keselowski, whose racing family was long identified with Dodge, could move to Kaulig, a scenario made possible when Keselowski announced several weeks ago that he would not return to RFK (Roush, Fenway, Keselowski), the Ford team that Keselowski partly owned.


Brad Keselowski at the NASCAR Cup Series Playoffs Xfinity 500 on October 31, 2026.


Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


It does not hurt Keselowski’s chances with Dodge that he delivered the brand its last Cup season championship back in 2012[when he drove for Roger Penske](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/keselowski-vacates-penske-seat-to-become-part-owner-of-roushs-nascar-race-team/) . Right after winning the championship, Dodge left NASCAR.


Aside from a driver lineup for both the Cup and FedEx Truck series (Craftsman, for the second time, is leaving as the series sponsor after Friday), two questions remain: One, Dodge has not announced what “car” it will run in the Cup series—though the differences in the Chevrolet, Ford, and Toyota Cup cars are mostly in the vinyl wraps that mimic the brands’ noses, taillights, and side window treatments. Dodge used to call its 2012 car a Charger, and we’ve seen the 2027 Dodge Charger, and that body style would certainly work. But we may also see the return of a much-updated Challenger.


Dodge / Kaulig Racing


That announcement will come on December 4 at Five Flags Speedway in Pensacola, Florida, home of the prestigious Snowball Derby race for late-model stock cars. There will also be a race there among identically prepared Dodge Charger race cars with “celebrity drivers” behind the wheel. The company already went to that well for Kaulig’s fifth Ram race truck this past season, where guest drivers—including Tony Stewart, Travis Pastrana, Regan Smith, Conor Daly, and Ryan Newman—split time racing the number 25 Ram.


The second big question hovering over Dodge’s Cup program for 2027: What engine will they use? The strongest rumor is that the Dodge will run a V-8 engine built by ECR, or Earnhardt Childress Racing, which builds Chevrolet V-8s for Richard Childress Racing and a few other cars in the Cup series, as well as Chevrolet engines for the O’Reilly series. ECR builds the Chevy engines that Kaulig uses in its Chevrolet Cup cars at present; I’ve been told that NASCAR, which has always required manufacturers to develop their own V-8 engines (though they share more and more parts each year, it seems), will allow ECR to slightly modify the Chevrolets it builds to at least resemble a Dodge product.


That still seems like a real stretch. Perhaps Dodge has pledged to build its own engine ASAP, or maybe NASCAR is convinced that any fan backlash won’t be that bad, and balanced out by what Dodge will contribute to NASCAR’s bottom line, and what the brand will spend promoting its return to NASCAR Cup racing.


Meg Oliphant/Getty Images


If Dodge’s Tim Kuniskis has any reservations about how hand-to-mouth the race program may seem right now, it doesn’t show. In a statement released at[the SEMA show](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema-2026/) in Las Vegas, he said this: “Everyone said it was impossible to get back in one year. We said, ‘Watch this.’ Sure, we could spend three years planning, testing, and perfecting… or we could do all three in real time, on the track. It’s going to be exponentially harder this way. But slow has never been part of Dodge DNA. LFG.”


Which translates, of course, to *“Let’s F-ing Go.”* Yeah, they’d better.


The post[It’s Official: Dodge Will Jump Back into NASCAR Cup Racing](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/its-official-dodge-will-jump-back-into-nascar-cup-racing/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
